3613.dq: Il est évident que le type de pied qu'on observe dans les langues mandé est différent de celui dans des langues à accent (« le pied métrique »). Le type mandé peut être défini par le terme anglais « featural foot », proposé par Green (2015); en français, on peut traduire ce terme par « pied caractéristique ».

3613.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Word stress is neither located nor denied.

3613.tone: Five level tonemes plus three falling tones; 'Le ton joue un rôle grammatical très important en dan-gouèta' (extra-low tone marks neutral aspect on verbs and the head noun of a genitive construction; tonal changes mark plural/intensive of adjectives; a floating extra-low tonal suffix marks the infinitive/prohibitive and an elided 3sg pronoun). Tone domain is the syllable; the rhythmic unit is the foot. The only remark touching accent is fn. 6, which says the Mande foot differs from the metric foot of 'langues à accent'; no sentence locates, describes or denies word stress. Vydrin 2016 (open, English, saved) concurs: 'The domain of a tone is the syllable. Another important rhythmic unit in Dan is the metric foot'.

tn.quote: Le dan-gouèta a cinq tonèmes simples, essentiellement réalisés comme tons unis: 1) extra-haut: ka̋a ‘gale’; 2) haut: káa ‘vous’ ...; 3) moyen: kāa ‘vous’ ...; 4) bas: kàa ‘gratter’ ...; 5) extra-bas: kȁa ‘roseau’. S’y ajoute trois tons modulés: 1) haut – descendant: gbân ‘fourmi grosse noire’; 2) moyen – descendant: dīn̏ ‘faim’ (un ton rare); 3) extra-haut – descendant: tö ‘arbre à bois très mou’, zīizïdhȅ ‘très-très ancien’, bhëbhë ‘extrêmement bon, excellent’ (un ton rare ...). Le ton joue un rôle grammatical très important en dan-gouèta.
tn.translation: Dan-Gouèta has five simple tonemes, essentially realised as level tones: 1) extra-high: ka̋a 'scabies'; 2) high: káa 'you (pl.)' ...; 3) mid: kāa 'you (pl.)' ...; 4) low: kàa 'scratch' ...; 5) extra-low: kȁa 'reed'. To these are added three modulated tones: 1) high-falling: gbân 'big black ant'; 2) mid-falling: dīn̏ 'hunger' (a rare tone); 3) extra-high-falling: tö 'tree with very soft wood', zīizïdhȅ 'very very old', bhëbhë 'extremely good, excellent' (a rare tone ...). Tone plays a very important grammatical role in Dan-Gouèta.

3615.dq: 倒话里除四个声调外，还有轻声现象，主要是各种语法标志中的一些音节，轻声在本书中不标调；在自然语流中，还有变调现象。 (tones are lexical citation-form syllable tones; toneless syllables are grammatical markers; no word- or phrase-level stress domain is described)
3615.dloc: 第一章 第二节 二、语音系统概述 (三) 声调, book pp.15-16 (image scan); cf. book p.249 and book p.50, (三) 倒话声调与藏、汉语言声调的比较及其疑问.
3615.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Daohua is described as a syllable-tone language with four lexical tone categories on full syllables (1 高平降 554, 2 中平降 332, 3 高降 51, 4 中降升 324, corresponding to the yinping/yangping/shang/qu categories of the Chinese-derived vocabulary), grouped into a high register (A, C) and a low/mid register (B, D); vowel length is a concomitant of tone (A, D long; B, C short). Besides the four tones there are toneless (轻声) syllables, mainly grammatical markers, and tone sandhi (变调) in connected speech.
3615.quote: 倒话共有四个声调调类。其具体调类调值为（按倒话中汉语词的阴阳上去排例）：1调：高平降554；2调：中平降332；3调：高降51；4调：中降升324。为了简明起见，在文中以各调调号标调，不标调值。例字：... 说明：1）倒话的声调又可以分为高、低（或高、中）两组，A、C两调可称为高调，B、D两调可称为低（中）调。这样分组之后还可以发现每组内部各有长短调的不同：A、D两调即又表现为长调，B、C两调又表现为短调。倒话元音长短可以视为不同声调的伴随特征。2）倒话里除四个声调外，还有轻声现象，主要是各种语法标志中的一些音节，轻声在本书中不标调；在自然语流中，还有变调现象。[p.249] 在倒话的声调分析时，由于倒话的两个源语言的声调格局非常类似，难以分析其要素和结构源流；而在五屯话这里，由于源语言在这方面的巨大差别，为我们提供了观察语音系统整合的绝佳机会。
3615.loc: 第一章 第二节 二、语音系统概述 (三) 声调, book pp.15-16 (image scan); cf. book p.249 and book p.50, (三) 倒话声调与藏、汉语言声调的比较及其疑问.

3615.tone: Four-tone syllable-tone system (554, 332, 51, 324) with high/low register grouping and tone-conditioned vowel length; toneless (轻声) grammatical-marker syllables; tone sandhi in connected speech. Instrumental F0 contours and mean durations per tone (224/192/160/282 ms, one female speaker of 雅江县河口镇城厢村, b.1974, recorded 2000, analysed 2001 at Nankai) on pp.16-18. Book p.50 table 2.2 aligns the Daohua tones with Chengdu Mandarin and Dege Kham Tibetan and says all three tone systems are close. The book contains no statement about word stress (重音) for Daohua: every 重音/'声调重音' passage (book pp.214, 242-248) concerns Wutun (五屯话, wutu1241), and p.249 contrasts Daohua, whose two source languages have very similar tone systems, with Wutun, whose Amdo Tibetan source lacks tone. 轻声 is also used on book p.27 (the strings of verbal suffixes mostly have no fixed tone, vary with the neighbouring elements and intonation, and are mostly treated as 轻声 and left unmarked); the p.13 footnote 轻声 concerns Lhasa/Batang Tibetan 'diphthongs', not Daohua.

3619.dloc: Chapter 3, sec. 3.4 Tone and 3.4.1 'Is Dauro a tone language?', pp. 58-60; minimal pairs (82)-(84) pp. 60-61; conclusion p. 63.
3619.prule: No stress rule is stated. Dauro is analysed as a register tone language with two level tones, high and low; at the surface the tone of the first syllable persists through the whole word (words are all-high or all-low), and the contrast is lexical (k'éesáa 'colostrum' vs k'eesaa 'priest', háitsáa 'leaf' vs haitsaa 'ear', mátsáa 'bee' vs matsaa 'milk') and grammatical (zóɁó 'red things' vs zoɁo 'red', Ɂádússá 'lengthened' vs Ɂadussa 'long', púnná 'blow' vs punna 'something blown'). No syllable is ever identified as stressed.

3619.tone: The thesis uses 'stress' once, generically (p. 46: 'phonological properties like stress and tone take syllable as their domain'), and 'accent' only for the acute tone mark (p. 60) and in the review of earlier work (p. 8: Allan 1976 'has tried to show supra-segmental features like vowel length, gemination, and pitch accent'). It quotes Allan (1976: 332), 'while there are two levels of systematic pitch in [Dauro], for the most part, pitch is predictable and non-contrastive', and reads this as denying tone; Siseraw (1989) is reported as finding two level tones with most words ending low. Tariku's own analysis (highland/Gok'a dialect, citation forms in isolation): register tone, two level tones H and L, realized as rising or falling pitch across the whole word, with lexical and grammatical function. The second-hand pairs in Alebachew 2010:10-11 and Hanserud 2018:15 (from Allan 1976 and Siseraw 1989: bàná 'I will go'/báná 'dust', dùtsá 'tail'/dútsà 'part torn off', sadyà 'foot'/sadyá 'country') put H on different syllables of a word, unlike Tariku's whole-word H/L, and Hirut 2004:26 calls the described Ometo languages (Wolaitta, Zayse, Gamo, Haro) tone-accent languages with one H per simple word. Whether Dawro is a two-tone language or a one-H-per-word tone-accent language is left open; Hanserud 2018:16 says Alebachew 'concludes that the question of tone vs. pitch is understudied in Dawro'. Either way no source states a stress position.

3623.prule: No word-stress rule. Dendi (with Zarma) is classified as Nicolaï's prosodic Type 4: a tonal system with four syllable-level distinctions (high, low, rising, falling), reducible in most cases to two tone values (H, L) by a mora analysis; the tone patterns of polysyllables and of words in combination are rule-governed. Accent systems (Types 1-3) exist only in Western, Eastern and Northern Songhay. For the tonal dialects, intensity is a redundant auxiliary feature riding on the high tone, preferentially on the word-initial syllable, with closed syllables holding it better (stated for Kaado, declared valid for the other tonal systems).
3623.quote: Type 4: Système tonal permettant quatre distinctions dans le cadre syllabique {CV́, CV̀, CV̌, CV̂}.
